issues.legal_issue: A party may be permitted to lead secondary evidence when foundational facts account for the original document’s non-production and evidence supports its existence, even if its existence has not been conclusively established before that evidence is received.
material_facts: The appellants sought to prove a copy of a will after the original, which they said had been given to revenue officials, could not be produced.
The officials failed to produce the original after receiving court-issued notices to do so, but neither unequivocally denied that it existed.

One official testified that he could not trace it, in part because the matter was old and he was no longer posted in that area; another acknowledged that a will had been handed to an official for mutation purposes.
The will’s scribe identified it and testified that it bore his signature as scribe and witness.
issues.conclusion: The foundational factual basis for secondary evidence had been established, and the appellants had to be given an opportunity to lead it. The refusal to permit secondary evidence was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 65(a) and 66 of the Evidence Act, secondary evidence may be given when the original appears to be held by a person legally bound to produce it and is not produced after notice. A party must establish foundational facts explaining why the original is unavailable. Ashok Dulichand v. Madahavlal Dube and Rakesh Mohindra v. Anita Beri address the conditions for secondary evidence; H. Siddiqui v. A. Ramalingam confirms that a plausible reason for non-production and a factual foundation are required. The court must assess the evidence bearing on the original’s existence and non-production; conclusive proof of the document is not a precondition to allowing the secondary evidence to be led.

rule.if: civil_evidence_appeal and original_not_produced_after_notice and evidence_supports_original_existence and nonproduction_reason_explained

predicates.civil_evidence_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a refusal to permit a party to lead secondary evidence in a civil case.
predicates.original_not_produced_after_notice: A person appearing to hold the original document did not produce it after receiving notice to do so.
predicates.evidence_supports_original_existence: Testimony or other evidence supports that the original document existed.
predicates.nonproduction_reason_explained: Evidence gives a reason why the original document was not produced.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges refusal of secondary evidence and the original was not produced after notice, evidence supports its existence, and its non-production is explained, the output is that secondary evidence must be permitted.

issues.legal_issue: Admission of secondary evidence does not by itself establish the authenticity, truthfulness, or genuineness of the document.
material_facts: The appellants were permitted to lead secondary evidence of a copy of the will.
The Court clarified that the document’s authenticity, truthfulness, and genuineness would still have to be established at trial.
issues.conclusion: Permission to lead secondary evidence does not automatically prove the document; its authenticity, truthfulness, and genuineness must be established during trial in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: The admission of a document into evidence, including its marking as an exhibit, does not by itself prove it. The document must be proved in accordance with law; permission to use secondary evidence only allows that evidence to be led.

predicates.secondary_evidence_offered: A party offers secondary evidence of a document in a court proceeding.

issues.definition: When secondary evidence of a document is offered, the document still requires proof of its authenticity.
